set1.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
set1.q: A 49-year-old man is discharged after receiving a mechanical aortic valve. Which medication must he be told he will take for life?
opts: Nitroprusside
Nitroprusside is an intravenous vasodilator used briefly in intensive care for acute aortic regurgitation. A mechanical valve needs lifelong warfarin.
Warfarin
Correct. A mechanical valve of titanium and carbon needs lifelong anticoagulation, and warfarin, the most commonly used vitamin K antagonist, is recommended for long-term management.
Aspirin
Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent, and vitamin K antagonist therapy is recommended over antiplatelet agents for a mechanical valve. Warfarin is the lifelong drug.
Heparin
Heparin is only a bridge when warfarin has to stop for surgery. The medication for life after a mechanical valve is warfarin.

set1.q: A 19-year-old woman is found to have a mid-systolic click at the apex at a sports physical. She feels well. Which is the most appropriate initial test?
opts: Chest radiograph
A chest radiograph does not show the leaflets or their motion. A mid-systolic click is investigated with an echocardiogram showing redundant leaflets.
Echocardiogram
Correct. Mitral valve prolapse is diagnosed by echocardiogram, which shows thickened, redundant mitral leaflets greater than 5 mm bowing into the left atrium during systole.
Cardiac catheterization
Catheterization is invasive and not how prolapse is diagnosed. An echocardiogram shows the thickened, redundant mitral leaflets.
Electrocardiogram
An electrocardiogram does not show valve anatomy. The diagnosis of mitral valve prolapse is made by echocardiogram.

set1.q: A 45-year-old man with known pulmonic regurgitation now has fatigue, ankle edema, distended neck veins and ascites. Which process explains these findings?
opts: Right-sided heart failure

Correct. Retrograde flow from the pulmonary artery overloads the right ventricle, and the symptoms of pulmonic regurgitation are those of right-sided heart failure: fatigue, peripheral edema, jugular venous distension and ascites.
Left-sided heart failure
Left-sided failure causes orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea and rales. Edema, distended neck veins and ascites from a pulmonic lesion are right-sided failure.
Low-output hypotension
His findings are congestive, not low-output. Right ventricular overload from pulmonic regurgitation produces right-sided heart failure with edema and ascites.
Pulmonary edema only
Pulmonary edema is the congestion of left-sided failure. Peripheral edema, neck vein distension and ascites mean right-sided heart failure.

set1.q: A 53-year-old woman with mitral stenosis and an enlarged left atrium now has an irregularly irregular pulse from atrial fibrillation. Which complication does this rhythm place her at risk for?
opts: Thromboembolism

Correct. Left atrial enlargement in mitral stenosis predisposes to atrial fibrillation, and atrial fibrillation is a risk factor for thromboembolism. That is why the rhythm matters beyond the palpitations.
Aortic dissection
Aortic dissection is a cause of acute aortic regurgitation and of root disease. The risk that follows atrial fibrillation in mitral stenosis is thromboembolism.
Papillary muscle rupture
Papillary muscle rupture follows an acute myocardial infarction and causes acute mitral regurgitation. Atrial fibrillation in mitral stenosis raises the risk of thromboembolism.
Carotid radiation of the murmur
Radiation to the carotids describes the aortic stenosis murmur, not a complication. Atrial fibrillation in mitral stenosis raises the risk of thromboembolism.

set1.q: A 44-year-old woman with mitral stenosis has breathlessness on exertion and orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat). Her valve area is 1.3 cm2, so the stenosis is not yet severe. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Hydralazine
Hydralazine is one of the afterload reducers for chronic aortic regurgitation. The medical treatment for dyspnea and orthopnea in mitral stenosis is a loop diuretic.
Balloon valvotomy
Percutaneous balloon valvotomy is surgical treatment for severe mitral stenosis (area below 1.0 cm2) with symptoms or pulmonary hypertension. Her area of 1.3 cm2 is not yet severe.
No therapy
No therapy is the plan only when mitral stenosis is asymptomatic with sinus rhythm. She has dyspnea and orthopnea, which call for a loop diuretic.
A loop diuretic

Correct. Mitral stenosis with symptoms of dyspnea and orthopnea is treated medically with a loop diuretic such as furosemide or bumetanide. Surgery waits for severe stenosis with symptoms or pulmonary hypertension.

set1.q: A 14-year-old girl with a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border has an electrocardiogram before cardiology review. Which finding is most expected?
opts: Right axis deviation
Correct. Pulmonic stenosis raises right ventricular pressure, and the electrocardiogram shows right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy.
Left atrial abnormality
Left atrial abnormality is the electrocardiogram of mitral stenosis. Pulmonic stenosis loads the right ventricle and shows right axis deviation.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is the electrocardiogram of severe aortic stenosis and chronic aortic regurgitation. Pulmonic stenosis shows right axis deviation.
Isolated right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement out of proportion to right ventricular hypertrophy is tricuspid stenosis. Pulmonic stenosis shows right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy.

set1.q: A 27-year-old woman has echocardiogram-confirmed pulmonic stenosis that is mild. She has no symptoms and asks about her outlook. Which is the most appropriate counseling?
opts: She will need lifelong warfarin
Lifelong warfarin is for a mechanical heart valve. Mild pulmonic stenosis needs no treatment and carries an excellent 20-year survival.
Survival is about two years
About two years is the untreated survival once aortic stenosis causes heart failure. Mild pulmonic stenosis has 94% survival at 20 years.
No treatment; survival is excellent
Correct. Mild to moderate pulmonic stenosis needs no treatment, and survival is 94% at 20 years. Intervention is reserved for severe disease with symptoms.
Balloon valvuloplasty is needed now
Pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty is for severe pulmonic stenosis with symptoms. Mild disease needs no treatment and has 94% survival at 20 years.

set1.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
set1.q: A 60-year-old man with a mechanical aortic valve on warfarin is scheduled for a colectomy that requires stopping it. Which plan should be avoided?
opts: Resuming a vitamin K antagonist
A mechanical valve needs lifelong vitamin K antagonist therapy, so resuming warfarin after surgery is required. The error is stopping it without a heparin bridge.
Stopping warfarin with no bridge

Correct. If surgery requires interrupting warfarin, it must be bridged with heparin until the international normalized ratio is therapeutic; leaving a mechanical valve uncovered is the thing to avoid.
Bridging with heparin
Heparin bridging is exactly what is required when surgery interrupts warfarin in a patient with a mechanical valve. The plan to avoid is stopping warfarin with no cover.
Rechecking his ratio after surgery
Warfarin is bridged until the international normalized ratio is therapeutic again, so rechecking it is part of the plan. What must be avoided is an unbridged gap.

set1.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
set1.q: A 70-year-old woman has mechanical valves in both the aortic and mitral positions. Which target international normalized ratio is recommended?
opts: A ratio of 3.5 is the top of the range for valves in both positions, not the target. The target is 3.0.
Correct. Mechanical valves in both the aortic and mitral positions target an international normalized ratio of 3.0, range 2.5 to 3.5 -- when two targets differ, go with the higher one.
A target of 2.5 applies to a single mechanical aortic valve. With a mechanical mitral valve as well, the target rises to 3.0.
A ratio of 2.0 is the bottom of the aortic range only. Valves in both positions target 3.0, range 2.5 to 3.5.

set1.q: A 42-year-old woman has tricuspid stenosis seen on an echocardiogram and mild leg swelling. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: No follow-up needed
Tricuspid stenosis on an echocardiogram with heart failure related symptoms is referred to cardiology rather than dismissed.
Mechanical replacement
Replacement is for severe symptomatic disease, and when done, a bioprosthetic valve is preferred. The first step for her is cardiology referral.
Balloon valvotomy now
Balloon valvotomy is reserved for hepatic congestion or severe venous congestion. Tricuspid stenosis seen on echo is first referred to cardiology.
Cardiology referral
Correct. Tricuspid stenosis is referred when it is seen on an echocardiogram or when there are heart failure related symptoms, both of which she has.

set1.q: A 72-year-old man with worsening tricuspid regurgitation from pulmonary hypertension is being followed. Which symptoms mark that his regurgitation has become severe?
opts: Hoarseness and dysphagia
Hoarseness and dysphagia come from an enlarged left atrium in mitral stenosis. Severe tricuspid regurgitation causes pedal edema and ascites.
Exertional angina and syncope
Exertional angina and syncope are cardinal symptoms of aortic stenosis. Severe tricuspid regurgitation shows pedal edema and ascites.
Hemoptysis and orthopnea
Hemoptysis and orthopnea reflect high left atrial pressure in mitral stenosis. Severe tricuspid regurgitation causes pedal edema and ascites.
Pedal edema and ascites
Correct. Mild to moderate tricuspid regurgitation is usually asymptomatic; severe disease causes pedal edema and ascites from right-sided congestion.

set1.q: A 26-year-old woman with echocardiogram-confirmed mitral valve prolapse has no symptoms and no murmur. She is worried about her heart. Which is the most appropriate counseling?
opts: Usually benign; no treatment is needed
Correct. Mitral valve prolapse is usually benign and asymptomatic, and usually no treatment is necessary. Intervention is considered only if it progresses to mitral regurgitation.
Lifelong warfarin to prevent clots
Lifelong warfarin is for mechanical heart valves. Uncomplicated mitral valve prolapse is usually benign and needs no treatment.
Avoid all exercise for life
Exercise restriction is the advice for aortic stenosis, which is preload dependent. Mitral valve prolapse is usually benign with no treatment needed.
Plan an early valve replacement
Replacement is considered only if prolapse progresses to mitral regurgitation. Asymptomatic prolapse is usually benign and needs no treatment.

set1.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
set1.q: A 71-year-old woman with severe aortic stenosis needs valve replacement. She has had repeated major bleeding, and anticoagulation is contraindicated. Which valve type is preferred?
opts: No valve replacement
Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis carries a 75% three-year mortality, so declining surgery leaves that risk untreated. Choosing a biological valve removes the need for anticoagulation.
Bioprosthetic valve
Correct. Bioprosthetic valves are preferred when there is any contraindication to anticoagulation; they do not need anticoagulation beyond the immediate postoperative period.
Mechanical valve
A mechanical valve of titanium and carbon needs lifelong anticoagulation, which she cannot take. A biological valve avoids long-term anticoagulation.
Balloon valvuloplasty
Percutaneous aortic balloon valvuloplasty is the option for children and young adults, not a valve replacement. With anticoagulation contraindicated she needs a biological valve.

set1.q: A 41-year-old man has an echocardiogram showing a dilated aortic root with mild aortic regurgitation. He feels well. Which is the most appropriate plan?
opts: Reassurance with no follow-up
A dilated aortic root is a cause of aortic regurgitation and can progress. It should be monitored by a cardiologist rather than dismissed.
Emergency valve replacement
Emergency replacement is for acute severe aortic regurgitation with shock or pulmonary edema. A well patient with a dilated root and mild leak is monitored by cardiology.
Annuloplasty of the tricuspid valve
Annuloplasty treats tricuspid regurgitation caused by annular dilation. The dilated aortic root in this patient is monitored by a cardiologist.
Ongoing monitoring by cardiology

Correct. Patients with a dilated aortic root should be monitored by a cardiologist, and a patient with an audible regurgitant murmur should have a cardiology consult to decide whether follow-up is needed.

set1.q: A 47-year-old woman with tricuspid stenosis has right upper quadrant pain. Examination finds a tender, enlarged liver. Which explains her pain?
opts: A dilated aortic root
A dilated aortic root causes aortic regurgitation and does not produce liver pain. Tricuspid stenosis congests the liver.
Congestion of an enlarged liver

Correct. Obstructed inflow from the right atrium to the right ventricle backs blood into the venous system, causing portal congestion; right upper quadrant pain in severe tricuspid stenosis comes from the enlarged liver.
Low cardiac output to the gut
Low cardiac output in tricuspid stenosis explains the cold skin. The right upper quadrant pain is the enlarged, congested liver.
Gallstones from carcinoid
Carcinoid disease is a cause of tricuspid stenosis, not of gallstones. Her pain comes from portal congestion and an enlarged liver.

set1.q: A 39-year-old woman who emigrated from a country where rheumatic fever is common has breathlessness on exertion and orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat). A diastolic rumble is heard at the apex. Which is the most appropriate initial test?
opts: Cardiac catheterization
Cardiac catheterization is not necessary for mitral stenosis and is usually done for an ischemic evaluation. The test that answers her symptoms is a transthoracic echocardiogram.
Electrocardiogram only
An electrocardiogram may show left atrial abnormality or atrial fibrillation, but it does not show the valve. Suggestive symptoms call for an echocardiogram.
No test until symptoms worsen
She already has suggestive symptoms, and dyspnea on exertion or orthopnea is the trigger for an echocardiogram. Waiting would miss a treatable stenosis.
Transthoracic echocardiogram
Correct. Any patient with symptoms suggestive of mitral stenosis, such as dyspnea on exertion or orthopnea, should get an echocardiogram. It shows a large left atrium and the stenotic mitral valve.

set1.q: A 69-year-old woman has severe mitral regurgitation. Which electrocardiogram finding is most expected?
opts: Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy is the pulmonic stenosis electrocardiogram. Severe mitral regurgitation shows left atrial enlargement.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement out of proportion to right ventricular hypertrophy is the tricuspid stenosis pattern. Mitral regurgitation enlarges the left atrium.
An expected normal tracing
Severe mitral regurgitation dilates the left atrium under volume and pressure load, so left atrial enlargement is the expected finding, not a normal tracing.
Left atrial enlargement
Correct. Severe mitral regurgitation shows left atrial enlargement and left ventricular hypertrophy on the electrocardiogram, though with low sensitivity and questionable specificity.

set1.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
set1.q: A 59-year-old woman has a mechanical aortic valve and takes warfarin. Which target international normalized ratio is recommended for her?
opts: A ratio of 4.0 is above the range for every mechanical valve position. The mechanical aortic target is 2.5, and the highest target, for mitral or both, is 3.0.
Correct. For a mechanical aortic valve the target international normalized ratio is 2.5, with a range of 2.0 to 3.0. A mechanical mitral valve, or valves in both positions, target 3.0.
A target of 3.0 (range 2.5 to 3.5) is for a mechanical mitral valve or mechanical valves in both positions. Her single aortic valve targets 2.5.
A ratio of 1.5 falls below the whole therapeutic range for any mechanical valve. The mechanical aortic target is 2.5, with a range of 2.0 to 3.0.

set1.q: A 24-year-old woman has an early diastolic murmur at the second left intercostal space from pulmonic regurgitation. Her history includes a balloon valvuloplasty at age 6 for right ventricular outflow obstruction. Which is the most likely cause of her regurgitation?
opts: Her prior valvuloplasty
Correct. Iatrogenic regurgitation, after surgical valvotomy, valvectomy or valvuloplasty to reduce right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, is the most common cause of pulmonic regurgitation.
Carcinoid disease
Carcinoid disease is a low-pressure cause of pulmonic regurgitation, but nothing in her history suggests it. Her prior valvuloplasty is the most common cause overall.
Rheumatic heart disease
Rheumatic heart disease is the leading cause of mitral stenosis and, worldwide, of tricuspid stenosis. Her pulmonic regurgitation follows her prior valvuloplasty.
Myxomatous degeneration
Myxomatous degeneration causes mitral valve prolapse. The most common cause of pulmonic regurgitation is iatrogenic, as after her valvuloplasty.

set1.q: A 33-year-old man with severe pulmonic stenosis awaiting valvuloplasty has ankle swelling and an enlarged liver from right heart failure. Which medication relieves these symptoms?
opts: Warfarin
Warfarin is lifelong anticoagulation for a mechanical valve and does nothing for edema. Right heart failure symptoms are relieved with a diuretic.
Nitroprusside
Nitroprusside is intravenous stabilization for acute severe aortic regurgitation in intensive care. His right heart failure is treated with a diuretic.
A diuretic
Correct. In severe symptomatic pulmonic stenosis, diuretics give symptomatic relief of right heart failure, alongside pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty for the valve itself.
A nitrate
Nitrates are named in this topic only as a drug to avoid in aortic stenosis. Right heart failure symptoms in pulmonic stenosis are relieved with a diuretic.

set1.q: A 63-year-old woman with acute severe aortic regurgitation from endocarditis is waiting for valve surgery that is delayed by several hours. Which is the most appropriate temporary stabilization in the intensive care unit?
opts: Oral hydralazine and discharge home
Oral afterload reduction is chronic outpatient therapy. Acute severe regurgitation awaiting surgery is stabilized in intensive care with intravenous diuretics and nitroprusside.
Percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty
Balloon valvuloplasty relieves stenosis in children and young adults; it does not stabilize a leaking valve. The bridge to surgery is intravenous diuretics and nitroprusside.
Intravenous diuretics and nitroprusside

Correct. If surgery for acute severe aortic regurgitation is delayed, temporary stabilization may be attempted in the intensive care unit with intravenous diuretics and a vasodilator such as nitroprusside.
A fluid bolus to raise her preload
Adding volume worsens the pulmonary edema of acute regurgitation. Temporary stabilization uses intravenous diuretics and a vasodilator such as nitroprusside.

set1.q: A 21-year-old woman has pulmonic stenosis seen incidentally on an echocardiogram. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Refer to a cardiologist
Correct. Whether congenital or related to heart failure, pulmonic stenosis present on echocardiogram should be referred to a cardiologist.
Balloon valvuloplasty now
Balloon valvuloplasty is for severe pulmonic stenosis with symptoms. An incidental finding is first referred to a cardiologist.
No further evaluation
Pulmonic stenosis on an echocardiogram is referred to a cardiologist, congenital or not, even though mild disease needs no treatment.
Start lifelong warfarin
Warfarin is for mechanical heart valves, not a native stenotic valve. The step for pulmonic stenosis on echocardiogram is cardiology referral.

set1.q: A 40-year-old woman with no cardiac symptoms is found to have pulmonic regurgitation. Which is the most common way this lesion comes to attention?
opts: Syncope during strenuous exercise
Exertional syncope is a cardinal symptom of aortic stenosis. Pulmonic regurgitation is usually an incidental echo or examination finding.
Sudden shock and pulmonary edema
Shock with pulmonary edema is the picture of acute severe aortic regurgitation. Pulmonic regurgitation is usually discovered incidentally.
An incidental echo or exam finding
Correct. Pulmonic regurgitation is usually an incidental finding on an echocardiogram or on physical examination; the murmur is soft and hard to hear.
Chest pain with a new infarction
Chest pain with an infarction is how acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture presents. Pulmonic regurgitation is usually found incidentally.

set1.q: An 80-year-old man has exertional syncope. Echocardiogram shows an aortic valve area of 0.7 cm2, a mean gradient of 52 mmHg, a jet velocity of 4.6 m/s and symptomatic left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement

Correct. Surgery is indicated for severe aortic stenosis (below 1, above 40, above 4) with symptomatic left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Medical treatment is not effective and is for mild and moderate disease only.
Nitrates and a beta blocker
Medical therapy is not effective in aortic stenosis, and nitrates and beta blockers are on its avoid list because he is preload dependent. Severe symptomatic disease needs valve replacement.
Percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty
Percutaneous aortic balloon valvuloplasty is the option for children and young adults. An 80-year-old with severe symptomatic disease is treated with valve replacement.
Repeat echocardiogram in one year
Watching is not appropriate once aortic stenosis is severe and symptomatic; the prognosis worsens sharply after symptoms begin. He meets the indications for valve replacement.

set1.q: A 59-year-old man has a holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. He is asked to squeeze a hand grip firmly for a minute while the examiner listens. How does the murmur change?
opts: It becomes diastolic
No maneuver moves a murmur from systole into diastole; mitral regurgitation stays holosystolic. Handgrip simply makes it louder.
It becomes louder
Correct. Squatting and handgrip increase the mitral regurgitation murmur: peripheral vascular resistance to ventricular ejection rises and pushes more regurgitation back into the left atrium.
It becomes softer
Softening is the response of mitral regurgitation to standing or the Valsalva maneuver. Handgrip raises resistance to ejection and makes the murmur louder.
It does not change
Handgrip does change it: raising peripheral resistance to ejection augments regurgitation into the left atrium, so the murmur gets louder.

set1.q: A 79-year-old woman has a harsh systolic murmur at the second right intercostal space at the sternal border. Her physician palpates the apex and the carotid at the same time. Which combined finding suggests her stenosis is severe?
opts: Displaced apex with a collapsing pulse
A displaced point of maximal impulse and a collapsing pulse are aortic regurgitation findings. Severe stenosis gives a forceful apex with a delayed, weak carotid.
Normal apex with a brisk carotid pulse
A brisk carotid upstroke argues against severe obstruction. The clue to severe aortic stenosis is a forceful apex paired with a delayed, weakened carotid pulse.
Forceful apex with a delayed, weak carotid
Correct. Simultaneous palpation of a forceful left ventricular apex beat and a delayed, weakened carotid pulse is a bedside clue that severe aortic stenosis is present.
Weak apex with a bounding carotid pulse
Bounding pulses belong to aortic regurgitation, not stenosis. In severe aortic stenosis the apex is forceful and the carotid upstroke is delayed and weak.

set1.q: A 78-year-old man has chest pressure and lightheadedness when climbing stairs. He has a harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the second right intercostal space at the sternal border that radiates to both carotids. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation is a holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex that radiates to the axilla. Blowing means regurgitation, and this murmur is harsh and at the right upper sternal border.
Aortic regurgitation
Aortic regurgitation is a high-pitched blowing diastolic murmur at the third intercostal space on the left, radiating to the apex. This murmur is harsh and systolic, which is stenosis.
Aortic stenosis

Correct. Harsh means stenosis and systolic narrows it to the aortic or pulmonic valve; the second right intercostal space with radiation to the carotids places it at the aortic valve. Exertional angina and near-syncope are cardinal symptoms.
Pulmonic stenosis
Pulmonic stenosis is also harsh and systolic, but it sits at the left second to fourth intercostal space and grows louder with inspiration. It does not radiate to the carotids.

set1.q: A 74-year-old man has severe tricuspid regurgitation due to annular dilation from pulmonary hypertension. Beyond treating the underlying condition, which procedure is indicated?
opts: Valvotomy
Balloon valvotomy treats severe mitral stenosis, or tricuspid stenosis with hepatic congestion. Annular dilation causing regurgitation is treated with annuloplasty.
Mitral clip
A mitral valve clip treats severe mitral regurgitation. Tricuspid regurgitation from annular dilation is treated with annuloplasty.
Annuloplasty
Correct. Tricuspid regurgitation is treated by addressing the underlying condition, with annuloplasty when the regurgitation is due to annular dilation; repair or replacement is for a primary cause.
Valvuloplasty
Balloon valvuloplasty opens a stenotic valve, such as in severe pulmonic stenosis. A leak from annular dilation is treated with annuloplasty.

set1.q: A 67-year-old woman has severe mitral regurgitation with symptoms of left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Her ejection fraction is 52% and the left ventricular end-systolic dimension is 45 mm. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Percutaneous balloon valvotomy
Balloon valvotomy opens a stenotic mitral valve; it would not stop a leak. Severe symptomatic mitral regurgitation is treated with a clip or valve replacement.
A loop diuretic and yearly echo
Medical management alone is not enough once severe regurgitation has an ejection fraction below 60% and an end-systolic dimension above 40 mm. She meets the surgical indications.
Aortic valve replacement
Aortic valve replacement treats aortic stenosis or regurgitation. Her lesion is mitral, so the intervention is a mitral valve clip or replacement.
A mitral valve clip or replacement

Correct. Surgery is indicated for severe mitral regurgitation with symptomatic left ventricular systolic dysfunction, an ejection fraction below 60% or an end-systolic dimension above 40 mm. Options include a mitral valve clip or transcatheter mitral valve replacement.

set1.q: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis is in sinus rhythm. Which electrocardiogram finding is most expected?
opts: Left atrial abnormality

Correct. Mitral stenosis raises left atrial size and pressure, so the electrocardiogram shows left atrial abnormality. Atrial fibrillation is common in severe disease, and right ventricular hypertrophy appears with pulmonary hypertension.
Right axis deviation alone
Right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy is the electrocardiogram of pulmonic stenosis. Mitral stenosis shows left atrial abnormality first.
Right atrial enlargement only
Right atrial enlargement out of proportion to right ventricular hypertrophy is the tricuspid stenosis pattern. Mitral stenosis shows left atrial abnormality.
An expected normal tracing
Mitral stenosis enlarges the left atrium, and the electrocardiogram reflects that as left atrial abnormality. A normal tracing is not what is expected.

set2.q: A 22-year-old healthy woman has no symptoms. On a routine examination a mid-systolic click is heard at the apex with no murmur. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation is a holosystolic blowing murmur radiating to the axilla. A click with no murmur is prolapse, which may later progress to regurgitation.
Mitral valve prolapse
Correct. Mitral valve prolapse usually affects healthy women aged 15 to 30, is usually benign and asymptomatic, and gives a mid-systolic click at the apex as the leaflets flare into the left atrium.
Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis gives an opening snap and a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex, usually decades after rheumatic fever. A lone mid-systolic click is prolapse.
Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis is a harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the second right intercostal space, mostly in older adults. A mid-systolic click is prolapse.

set2.q: A 30-year-old man with known pulmonic stenosis now has exertional breathlessness and fatigue, and he fainted while running. Which process do these symptoms signal?
opts: Left atrial enlargement and fibrillation
Left atrial enlargement leading to atrial fibrillation is the course of mitral stenosis. Exertional symptoms in pulmonic stenosis mean severe disease with right heart failure.
Acute leak from papillary muscle rupture
Papillary muscle rupture after a myocardial infarction causes acute mitral regurgitation. His symptoms signal right heart failure from severe pulmonic stenosis.
A benign finding needing no action
Mild disease is benign, but syncope and exertional dyspnea mark severe pulmonic stenosis with right heart failure, which needs treatment.
Right heart failure from severe stenosis
Correct. Mild to moderate pulmonic stenosis is usually asymptomatic; severe disease produces right heart failure symptoms such as exertional dyspnea, fatigue, angina and syncope.

set2.q: A 16-year-old boy has a harsh, high-pitched crescendo-decrescendo mid-systolic ejection murmur at the left second to fourth intercostal spaces at the sternal border. It grows louder with inspiration, and the second heart sound is split. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pulmonic regurgitation
Pulmonic regurgitation sits at the second left intercostal space too, but it is a brief early diastolic decrescendo murmur. Harsh and systolic means stenosis.
Pulmonic stenosis

Correct. Harsh means stenosis and systolic narrows it to the aortic or pulmonic valve; the left upper sternal border, the inspiratory increase of a right-sided murmur and the split second sound mark pulmonic stenosis.
Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis is harsh and systolic but sits at the second right intercostal space, radiates to the carotids and is a left-sided murmur that is louder on expiration.
Tricuspid regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation also grows louder with inspiration, but it is holosystolic at the left lower sternal border near the epigastrium, not a harsh ejection murmur.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man with chronic mitral regurgitation has an echocardiogram showing a regurgitant fraction of 64%. Which severity does this indicate?
opts: Mild regurgitation
Mild mitral regurgitation is a regurgitant fraction below 30%. A fraction of 64% is severe.
Ungradeable by echocardiogram
Echocardiography grades mitral regurgitation by regurgitant fraction; left heart catheterization is not required. A fraction of 64% is severe.
Severe regurgitation
Correct. Mitral regurgitation is severe when the regurgitant fraction is 50% or more, meaning over half of the blood ejected goes backward. A fraction of 30 to 49% is moderate and below 30% is mild.
Moderate regurgitation
Moderate mitral regurgitation is a regurgitant fraction of 30 to 49%. At 64%, more than half of each beat leaks back, which is severe.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman with a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration is examined further. Which additional finding is most expected?
opts: Elevated jugular pulsations
Correct. Tricuspid regurgitation raises the jugular venous pressure with visible neck pulsations, and there may be a venous thrill (a palpable vibration) over the right jugular vein.
A collapsing radial pulse
A collapsing, water hammer pulse is the Corrigan pulse of aortic regurgitation. Tricuspid regurgitation gives an elevated jugular venous pressure with neck pulsations.
Delayed, weak carotid pulse
A delayed, weakened carotid with a forceful apex is the clue to severe aortic stenosis. Tricuspid regurgitation raises the jugular venous pressure.
Head bobbing with each beat
Head bobbing is the de Musset sign of aortic regurgitation. Tricuspid regurgitation gives elevated jugular pulsations and a venous thrill.

set2.q: A 64-year-old man, three days after an acute myocardial infarction, has sudden breathlessness, crackles in both lungs and a new holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. Which is the most likely cause?
opts: Papillary muscle rupture

Correct. An acute myocardial infarction with papillary muscle rupture is an acute cause of mitral regurgitation, and acute mitral regurgitation presents with left-sided heart failure symptoms such as dyspnea and rales.
Myxomatous degeneration
Myxomatous degeneration causes mitral valve prolapse, a chronic cause of mitral regurgitation. The sudden murmur three days after an infarction points to papillary muscle rupture.
Rheumatic heart disease
Rheumatic heart disease is a cause of mitral regurgitation, but it does not arrive suddenly three days after an infarction. Papillary muscle rupture does.
Tricuspid annular dilation
Tricuspid annular dilation causes tricuspid regurgitation in pulmonary hypertension, heard at the lower sternal border. An apical murmur after infarction is papillary muscle rupture.

set2.q: A 29-year-old man who injects drugs has fevers for two weeks. There is a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border near the epigastrium that grows louder with inspiration (Carvallo sign), and his neck veins pulsate. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Tricuspid regurgitation

Correct. A holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border near the epigastrium that increases with inspiration is tricuspid regurgitation; in an injection drug user the primary cause is infective endocarditis.
Mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation is holosystolic too, but it is at the apex radiating to the axilla and does not increase with inspiration. The Carvallo sign separates the two.
Tricuspid stenosis
Tricuspid stenosis is at the same location and also increases with inspiration, but it is a mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap, not a holosystolic murmur.
Pulmonic stenosis
Pulmonic stenosis is a harsh mid-systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border. A holosystolic murmur near the epigastrium is tricuspid regurgitation.

set2.q: A 50-year-old woman with mitral stenosis has worsening breathlessness. Echocardiogram shows a valve area of 0.8 cm2, a mean gradient of 14 mmHg and a peak velocity of 3.4 m/s. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Percutaneous balloon valvotomy

Correct. Her values are severe (area below 1.0 cm2, mean gradient above 10 mmHg, velocity above 3.0 m/s), and severe mitral stenosis with symptomatic dyspnea or pulmonary hypertension is an indication for percutaneous balloon valvotomy.
A loop diuretic indefinitely
A loop diuretic treats dyspnea and orthopnea, but severe mitral stenosis with symptoms meets the indication for intervention. The procedure is percutaneous balloon valvotomy.
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement treats severe aortic stenosis, a different valve. Severe symptomatic mitral stenosis is treated with percutaneous balloon valvotomy.
Afterload reduction with hydralazine
Afterload reduction is medical management for chronic aortic regurgitation. Severe symptomatic mitral stenosis needs percutaneous balloon valvotomy.

set2.q: A 34-year-old woman with mitral valve prolapse has now developed symptomatic severe mitral regurgitation with a falling ejection fraction. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: A mitral clip or valve replacement
Correct. Prolapse usually needs no treatment, but if it progresses to mitral regurgitation the options are a clip, transcatheter mitral valve replacement, or biological or mechanical replacement.
Reassurance with no treatment
Reassurance fits uncomplicated prolapse. Once it has progressed to symptomatic severe regurgitation, a clip or valve replacement is indicated.
Percutaneous balloon valvotomy
Balloon valvotomy treats severe mitral stenosis. A prolapsed valve that now leaks severely is treated with a clip or replacement.
Aortic valve replacement
Aortic valve replacement treats disease of the aortic valve. Prolapse that progresses to mitral regurgitation is treated at the mitral valve.

set2.q: A 35-year-old man has a brief early diastolic murmur at the second left intercostal space from pulmonic regurgitation. Which maneuver makes the murmur louder?
opts: Squatting
Correct. Anything that increases venous return increases the pulmonic regurgitation murmur -- inspiration, squatting and lying supine. Expiration and standing decrease it.
Standing
Standing reduces venous return, so it softens the pulmonic regurgitation murmur. Squatting, inspiration and lying supine make it louder.
Expiration
Expiration reduces venous return to the right heart and softens right-sided murmurs. Inspiration, squatting and lying supine make it louder.
Sitting upright
Sitting up does not add venous return the way lying supine does. Squatting, inspiration and the supine position increase the murmur.

set2.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
set2.q: A 58-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve asks whether she could take daily aspirin instead of her current anticoagulant. Which long-term therapy is recommended for her?
opts: Aspirin in place of it
Antiplatelet agents are specifically ranked below vitamin K antagonist therapy for a mechanical valve. Aspirin cannot replace her anticoagulant.
No drug after one year
A mechanical valve requires lifelong anticoagulation; it is biological valves that stop after the postoperative period. She stays on a vitamin K antagonist.
Heparin every day
Heparin bridges gaps in warfarin around surgery; it is not the long-term therapy. The recommendation is a vitamin K antagonist.
A vitamin K antagonist
Correct. With a mechanical heart valve, vitamin K antagonist therapy is recommended over no vitamin K antagonist and over antiplatelet agents. Warfarin is the one most commonly used.

set2.q: A 57-year-old man with hypertension has chronic aortic regurgitation, no symptoms and a preserved ejection fraction. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor

Correct. Chronic aortic regurgitation with preserved ejection fraction or no symptoms is managed medically with afterload reduction: an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker or hydralazine.
Emergency aortic valve replacement
Emergency replacement is for acute severe aortic regurgitation. Chronic disease with preserved ejection fraction and no symptoms is managed medically with afterload reduction.
Intravenous nitroprusside in intensive care
Intravenous nitroprusside is temporary stabilization for acute severe regurgitation awaiting delayed surgery. Chronic stable disease is treated with oral afterload reduction.
A loop diuretic and fluid restriction
Loop diuretics relieve dyspnea and orthopnea in mitral stenosis. The medical management named for chronic aortic regurgitation is afterload reduction.

set2.q: A 62-year-old woman has a holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. She stands up quickly from squatting while the examiner listens. How does the murmur change?
opts: It does not change
Standing does change it: the mitral regurgitation murmur decreases with standing or the Valsalva maneuver.
It gains a click
A mid-systolic click is the sign of mitral valve prolapse, not a response to a maneuver. Standing makes the mitral regurgitation murmur softer.
It becomes softer
Correct. The mitral regurgitation murmur decreases with standing or the Valsalva maneuver and increases with squatting and handgrip, which raise resistance to ventricular ejection.
It becomes louder
Louder is the response to squatting or handgrip, which raise resistance to ejection. Standing reduces the mitral regurgitation murmur.

set2.q: A 76-year-old man with known severe aortic stenosis has exertional chest pain. His physician is reviewing options before cardiology sees him. Which should be avoided for his chest pain?
opts: Staying well hydrated
Hydration protects preload, and dehydration and hypovolemia are what must be avoided in aortic stenosis. The dangerous choice is a nitrate, which drops preload.
Cardiology consultation
Every patient with aortic stenosis on echocardiogram should have a cardiology consult. That is recommended, not avoided; the agent to avoid is a nitrate.
Nitroglycerin

Correct. Patients with aortic stenosis are preload dependent, and nitrates drop preload. If angina is present in aortic stenosis, nitrates are avoided; the same logic removes dehydration and strenuous exertion.
Resting when pain starts
Resting is consistent with his care: strenuous physical activity is to be avoided in aortic stenosis. The agent to avoid is a nitrate, because it lowers the preload he depends on.

set2.q: A 68-year-old woman with aortic stenosis on echocardiogram plays competitive tennis and often skips fluids on hot days. She asks what she should change. Which advice is most appropriate?
opts: Restrict fluids to keep her volume low
Restricting fluids moves her toward hypovolemia, which is exactly what aortic stenosis patients must avoid. She needs to stay hydrated because she depends on preload.
Increase training to strengthen her heart
More strenuous exercise is the opposite of the advice. Strenuous physical activity and competitive sports are to be avoided in aortic stenosis, along with dehydration.
No changes until symptoms appear
Precautions start once the stenosis is known, not when symptoms arrive. She should stop competitive sports and avoid dehydration now, because she is preload dependent.
Avoid competitive sports and dehydration

Correct. Aortic stenosis makes the patient preload dependent, so she should avoid strenuous physical activity and competitive sports and avoid dehydration and hypovolemia, both of which reduce the preload she relies on.

set2.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
set2.q: A 63-year-old man with a mechanical mitral valve takes warfarin and needs elective abdominal surgery that requires stopping it. Which is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan?
opts: Double the warfarin
Surgery requires warfarin to be interrupted, not intensified. The accepted plan is to bridge with heparin until the international normalized ratio is therapeutic.
Bridge with heparin

Correct. If surgery requires a transition to heparin, warfarin must be bridged: heparin covers the gap until the international normalized ratio is therapeutic again. This matters most with a mechanical valve.
Stop all anticoagulation
A mechanical valve needs lifelong anticoagulation, and stopping warfarin without cover invites thrombus. The gap is covered by bridging with heparin.
Switch to aspirin alone
Vitamin K antagonist therapy is recommended over antiplatelet agents for a mechanical valve. Around surgery the cover is heparin until the ratio is therapeutic.

set2.q: A 66-year-old woman has tricuspid regurgitation identified on an echocardiogram and now has pedal edema and ascites. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Balloon valvotomy now
Balloon valvotomy opens stenotic valves and does not treat a leak. Tricuspid regurgitation on echo with right heart failure symptoms is referred.
Cardiology referral
Correct. Tricuspid regurgitation is referred when it is identified on echocardiogram or when there are right heart failure symptoms; pedal edema and ascites mark severe disease.
Reassure; mild disease
Pedal edema and ascites are the symptoms of severe tricuspid regurgitation, not mild. With echo findings and right heart failure symptoms she is referred.
Start lifelong warfarin
Warfarin is lifelong therapy for mechanical valves, not native tricuspid regurgitation. She needs cardiology referral.

set2.q: A 44-year-old woman has a mid-diastolic rumble at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration. Which electrocardiogram finding is most expected?
opts: Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy is pulmonic stenosis, where the right ventricle is pressure loaded. Tricuspid stenosis enlarges the right atrium.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy belongs to aortic stenosis and chronic aortic regurgitation. Tricuspid stenosis shows right atrial enlargement.
Right atrial enlargement
Correct. Tricuspid stenosis obstructs inflow from the right atrium to the right ventricle, so the electrocardiogram shows right atrial enlargement out of proportion to right ventricular hypertrophy.
Left atrial abnormality
Left atrial abnormality is the mitral stenosis electrocardiogram. Tricuspid stenosis dilates the right atrium instead.

set2.q: A 52-year-old woman has a diastolic blowing murmur at the left upper sternal border. An echocardiogram is ordered to find out why the valve leaks. Which finding would explain her regurgitation?
opts: Tricuspid annular dilation
Dilation of the tricuspid annulus is the most common cause of tricuspid regurgitation, in pulmonary hypertension. The echo finding that explains aortic regurgitation is root dilation or dissection.
Redundant mitral leaflets
Thickened, redundant mitral leaflets are the echo finding of mitral valve prolapse. For aortic regurgitation the echo looks for root dilation or dissection.
A narrowed, immobile mitral valve
Thick, immobile mitral leaflets with a narrowed orifice describe mitral stenosis. The cause of aortic regurgitation seen on echo is root dilation or dissection.
Aortic root dilation

Correct. Echocardiography is used to determine the cause of aortic regurgitation, such as aortic root dilation or aortic dissection. Root disease is one of the two main groups of causes, with valve disease.

set2.q: A 42-year-old woman who had rheumatic fever as a child has breathlessness on exertion. At the apex there is a low-pitched rumbling diastolic murmur that begins with an opening snap (a sharp sound just after the second heart sound), best heard with the bell in the left lateral decubitus position (lying on the left side). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Aortic regurgitation
Aortic regurgitation is diastolic but high-pitched and blowing, at the third intercostal space on the left. Blowing means regurgitation; this murmur is a low-pitched rumble.
Mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation is at the apex too, but it is a holosystolic blowing murmur radiating to the axilla. This murmur is diastolic and rumbling, which is stenosis.
Mitral stenosis

Correct. Rumble means stenosis and diastolic narrows it to the mitral or tricuspid valve; the apex, the opening snap after the second heart sound and the left lateral position mark mitral stenosis. Rheumatic heart disease is its most common cause.
Tricuspid stenosis
Tricuspid stenosis is also a diastolic rumble with an opening snap, but it sits at the left lower sternal border near the xiphoid and grows louder with inspiration. This murmur is at the apex.

set2.q: A 36-year-old woman has mitral stenosis found on an echocardiogram done before pregnancy. She has no symptoms and is in sinus rhythm. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Cardiology consultation

Correct. All patients with evidence of mitral stenosis on echocardiogram should have a cardiology consult to evaluate them and set the frequency of follow-up. Asymptomatic disease in sinus rhythm needs no therapy yet.
Start a loop diuretic
Loop diuretics treat dyspnea and orthopnea in mitral stenosis. With no symptoms and sinus rhythm she needs no therapy, but the echo finding still warrants a cardiology consult.
Balloon valvotomy now
Balloon valvotomy is for severe mitral stenosis with symptoms or pulmonary hypertension. An asymptomatic patient in sinus rhythm is referred to cardiology for evaluation.
No follow-up needed
Mitral stenosis on echocardiogram is not dismissed; it should have a cardiology consult to set follow-up. Only therapy, not referral, is withheld when she is asymptomatic.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man with chronic mitral regurgitation also has atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension. He is not yet a surgical candidate. Which is part of his medical management?
opts: Ignoring the rhythm for now
Atrial fibrillation is one of the comorbidities that medical management of mitral regurgitation specifically treats, along with pulmonary hypertension.
Treating his atrial fibrillation

Correct. Medical treatment of mitral regurgitation aims to increase forward cardiac output while reducing regurgitant volume, and to treat comorbidities such as atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension.
A nitrate to lower his preload
Avoiding nitrates is the preload rule for aortic stenosis. The named medical steps in mitral regurgitation are raising forward output and treating atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension.
Balloon valvotomy of the valve
Balloon valvotomy treats severe mitral stenosis, not a leaking valve. Medical care for mitral regurgitation treats the comorbid atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension.

set2.q: A 52-year-old woman has pulmonic regurgitation on echocardiogram and has developed leg edema and distended neck veins. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Repeat echo in 5 years
Deferring for years ignores her right heart failure. Pulmonic regurgitation on echo or with right heart failure signs is referred now.
Cardiology referral
Correct. Pulmonic regurgitation is referred when it is seen on echocardiogram or when there are right heart failure signs and symptoms, both of which she has.
No follow-up needed
An incidental leak may be quiet, but she now has right heart failure signs. Pulmonic regurgitation seen on echo or with right heart failure is referred.
Start lifelong warfarin
Warfarin is for mechanical heart valves. Pulmonic regurgitation with right heart failure signs is referred to cardiology.

set2.q: A 67-year-old woman has a holosystolic murmur, and the examiner is unsure whether it is tricuspid or mitral in origin. Which bedside maneuver best separates the two?
opts: Standing up quickly
Standing softens mitral regurgitation, but the maneuver that separates it from tricuspid regurgitation is inspiration, which increases the right-sided murmur.
Full expiration
Expiration increases left-sided murmurs, so it does not single out the tricuspid lesion. Inspiration makes tricuspid regurgitation louder and distinguishes it.
Deep inspiration
Correct. Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, so the tricuspid regurgitation murmur grows louder (the Carvallo sign) while mitral regurgitation does not. That distinguishes them.
Sustained handgrip
Handgrip raises resistance to ejection and makes mitral regurgitation louder, but it is not the maneuver named to separate the two. Inspiration increases only the tricuspid murmur.

set2.q: A 73-year-old woman with moderate aortic stenosis has blood pressure of 158/92 on repeated visits. Her clinician is choosing an antihypertensive. Which class should be avoided?
opts: An angiotensin receptor blocker

Angiotensin receptor blockers are not on the aortic stenosis avoid list, which names beta blockers and calcium channel blockers for hypertension; receptor blockers appear as afterload reducers in aortic regurgitation.
An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor

Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are not on the aortic stenosis avoid list; they are afterload reducers used in aortic regurgitation. The classes to avoid are beta blockers and calcium channel blockers.
Low-salt dietary counseling
Dietary counseling does not lower the preload she depends on and is not on any avoid list. The antihypertensive classes to avoid in aortic stenosis are beta blockers and calcium channel blockers.
A beta blocker
Correct. Aortic stenosis patients are preload dependent; if they have hypertension, beta blockers and calcium channel blockers are avoided, just as nitrates are avoided for angina.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man with chronic aortic regurgitation has no symptoms, but his echocardiogram now shows a reduced ejection fraction. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Continue afterload reduction alone
Afterload reduction is the medical management for aortic regurgitation with preserved ejection fraction. Once the ejection fraction falls, he is a surgical candidate even without symptoms.
Wait until symptoms develop
Waiting is not appropriate: chronic aortic regurgitation with a reduced ejection fraction makes him a surgical candidate whether or not he has symptoms.
Percutaneous balloon valvotomy
Balloon valvotomy treats severe symptomatic mitral stenosis. For aortic regurgitation with a reduced ejection fraction the step is evaluation for valve surgery.
Evaluation as a surgical candidate

Correct. Chronic aortic regurgitation with a mildly reduced or reduced ejection fraction, with or without symptoms, makes the patient a surgical candidate. Left untreated, survival is only about 2 to 3 years.

set2.q: A 46-year-old woman is diagnosed with severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis and asks what she can do at home. Which advice is most appropriate?
opts: Take daily aspirin
Aspirin is not part of tricuspid stenosis care, and antiplatelet therapy is ranked below a vitamin K antagonist even for mechanical valves. She should follow a low-salt diet.
Follow a low-salt diet
Correct. Severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis is managed with a low-salt diet together with diuretics and an aldosterone antagonist, which limits the systemic venous congestion.
Increase fluid and salt
More salt and fluid worsen the systemic venous congestion of tricuspid stenosis, which is why a low-salt diet with diuretics is the home measure.
Avoid all walking
Avoiding strenuous activity is the advice for preload-dependent aortic stenosis. The home measure for tricuspid stenosis is a low-salt diet.

set2.q: An 81-year-old man with a harsh systolic murmur has an echocardiogram showing an aortic valve area of 0.8 cm2, a mean gradient of 46 mmHg and a jet velocity of 4.3 m/s. Which severity do these values indicate?
opts: Ungradeable without catheterization
Echocardiography grades aortic stenosis by area, mean gradient and jet velocity. Catheterization gives definitive findings but is not required to call these numbers severe.
Severe aortic stenosis
Correct. Severe aortic stenosis is an area below 1.0 cm2, a mean gradient above 40 mmHg and a jet velocity above 4.0 m/s -- remembered as 4, 40 and 1. All three of his values cross those lines.
Moderate aortic stenosis
Moderate disease sits at an area of 1.0 to 1.5 cm2, a gradient of 25 to 40 mmHg and a velocity of 3.0 to 4.0 m/s. His values are past every one of those limits, so the grade is severe.
Mild aortic stenosis
Mild disease has an area above 1.5 cm2, a gradient below 25 mmHg and a velocity below 3.0 m/s. An area of 0.8 cm2 with a gradient of 46 mmHg is severe, not mild.

set2.q: A 51-year-old woman with long-standing mitral stenosis develops a hoarse voice and some difficulty swallowing. Which explains her hoarseness?
opts: Ruptured bronchial vein anastomoses
Rupture of small bronchial vein anastomoses under high left atrial pressure causes hemoptysis in mitral stenosis. Hoarseness comes from the atrium compressing the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
An enlarged liver from congestion
An enlarged, congested liver causes right upper quadrant pain in tricuspid stenosis. Hoarseness in mitral stenosis is the enlarged left atrium on the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
The enlarged left atrium on the nerve

Correct. Hoarseness in mitral stenosis (Ortner syndrome) comes from the enlarged left atrium impinging on the left recurrent laryngeal nerve; dysphagia comes from the atrium pressing on the esophagus.
A dilated aortic root on the trachea
A dilated aortic root is a cause of aortic regurgitation. In mitral stenosis the hoarseness comes from the enlarged left atrium pressing on the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.

set2.q: A 38-year-old woman raised in a region where rheumatic fever is common has a quivering discomfort in the neck, cold skin and right upper quadrant pain. There is a soft opening snap (a sharp sound just after the second heart sound) and a mid-diastolic rumble at the left lower sternal border near the xiphoid that grows louder with inspiration. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis is also an opening snap with a diastolic rumble, but it sits at the apex and is a left-sided murmur that does not grow with inspiration.
Tricuspid regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation is at the same location and also grows with inspiration, but it is holosystolic, not a diastolic rumble with an opening snap.
Pulmonic regurgitation
Pulmonic regurgitation is a brief early diastolic decrescendo at the second left intercostal space. A mid-diastolic rumble near the xiphoid is tricuspid stenosis.
Tricuspid stenosis

Correct. A rumble is stenosis and diastolic narrows it to the mitral or tricuspid valve; the left lower sternal border near the xiphoid and the inspiratory increase make it right-sided, so tricuspid stenosis. Rheumatic fever is its most common cause worldwide.
